They haven’t clinched a postseason berth yet, but it looks more likely by the day that the Boston Red Sox have a date with the New York Yankees in the Wild Card round again.
This will be the third matchup between these two arch rivals in the Wild Card round since 2021, with each organization winning once. The Red Sox got the best of Gerrit Cole in 2021 at Fenway Park, while the Yankees won two straight elimination games to knock off Boston in the Bronx last year.
This series promises to be low-scoring. These two teams are top three in baseball in staff earned run average. The Yankees have nearly three-quarters of a run lead on the Red Sox among starters, while the two bullpens are separated by 0.01 earned runs per nine.
A lot will be made of how these two staffs line up in a couple of weeks. The first two games for the Yankees, as deep as their pitching staff is, seem destined to be Cam Schlittler in Game 1 and Max Fried in Game 2. However, the Red Sox have serious questions to answer about how they want to line up.
Preparing for this series to go the distance is difficult. If you sweep, you line yourselves up well for Game 1 of the American League Division Series. However, if you get swept, one of your best pitchers may never see the hill.
The conundrum is as follows: Sonny Gray has been their best arm wire-to-wire. Payton Tolle is by far their hottest arm, seeming to get stronger as the season wears on. Ranger Suárez is riding two great starts in a row and is their high-priced free agent with elite postseason pedigree.
But of the three, there’s no question who should pitch opposite Schlittler in Game 1: Tolle.
Stats updated prior to games on September 19.
Game 1 Is a Tone-Setter
The dialogue surrounding Game 1 is that it’s almost a “scheduled loss.” To be frank, it’s hard to argue against the logic. In four starts against Boston this year, Schlittler has a 0.74 ERA, a .174 batting average against, and a 27.3% strikeout rate across 24.1 innings.
Let us not forget the sheer domination he exhibited in Game 3 against the Red Sox last year, either. Across eight innings, he allowed five hits, no runs, and struck out 12.
But the mindset for Boston can’t be that it has no chance of winning. Sure, they’ve been one of the league’s best road teams this year, but the Yankees have the best pitching staff in baseball this year for a reason. By comparison, sure, it’s easier to win against someone not in the Cy Young race. But Max Fried habitually finds himself in the discussion for a reason.
The Red Sox’s mindset should be that runs will be at a premium, so matching the Yankees ace zero-for-zero is paramount. Of the three options, Tolle presents the best opportunity to do so. While Gray has Tolle beat overall in ERA, the Red Sox rookie southpaw is, by far, the hottest arm on the staff.
Since the All-Star break, Tolle has a 2.90 ERA with a 28.2% strikeout-to-walk rate. That ERA drops to 2.53 over his last nine starts. That 2.90 ERA, however, is nearly a third of a run better than Gray’s, and over half a run better than Suárez’s.
Sheer run prevention is the name of the game in this series. Tolle is their best option.
Tolle’s Attitude Is Perfect for the Moment
Every time Tolle speaks, he endears himself to the baseball world even more. But as goofy as he can be in media sessions, he’s all business on the field. Furthermore, he can appreciate the moment he’s in at any given time.
Look no further than his recent start against the Kansas City Royals. Eight pitches, eight strikes, six whiffs, all fastballs. He had the wherewithal to glance at pitching coach Andrew Bailey, grin, lock back in and pick up the final strike of an immaculate inning.
Sure, it’s one pitch in the first inning against a team out of postseason contention, but talk to anybody who’s played, and they’ll tell you how aware they are of when they’re on the brink of something cool. Tolle said as much after the game.
But that moment should tell the world he’s unafraid of going into the Bronx, facing off against Schlittler, and going band-for-band with the likely AL Cy Young.
Tolle clearly cares about what he does, but it’s that somewhat unserious attitude that makes him perfect for the high stakes of setting the tone in a postseason series.
This moment, honestly, seemed set in stone the moment he made his MLB debut last season against Paul Skenes. While any postseason start is high leverage, he’s always finding himself making big starts against the game’s best. He’s always met the moment, and the Red Sox should let him continue that trend this postseason.
The Yankees Struggle Against Hard Fastballs
The Yankees are a deep, talented team even if not all players are at full strength or potential going into October. One area where they struggle, however, is against hard fastballs.
This season, the Yankees have the highest strikeout rate on fastballs 95 mph or harder, to go with the second-worst expected batting average. Only the Chicago White Sox are worse against such fastballs.
They’re even worse this season on hard fastballs thrown by left-handers. Their 33% strikeout rate is the second-highest behind the 61-93 Athletics, while their .191 expected batting average ranks only higher than the Cleveland Guardians.
Tolle isn’t positioned with an elite-level fastball from a velocity standpoint, but it’s comfortably above average. This season, he’s in the 71st percentile with an average fastball of 95.7 mph. Opponents struggle mightily against it as well, hitting just .190 with a .248 expected wOBA and a 30.4% whiff rate.
Tolle throws his four-seam and sinker a combined 68.4% of the time. While that leaves him susceptible to predictability, he varies that look with a cutter that comes in at 88.6 mph on average. He throws that offering at a 19.4% clip.
His strength is his fastball, along with 98th percentile extension. That plays directly into the weaknesses of the Yankees lineup. With Game 1 very much being a tone-setter, there’s no question who the Red Sox should send out there.
Lining It Up After Tolle
Following Tolle, the Red Sox have their two veterans waiting in the wings. Win Game 1, you’ve got two proven performers to help you win one more game to advance. Lose Game 1, you’ve got two experienced professionals tasked with staving off elimination.
The order after Tolle almost doesn’t matter. Could they vary looks and go to Gray to keep the Yankees off the lefty scent? Maybe, but then you potentially run into the same problem of playing with your food. That said, Suárez is much craftier than Tolle, and prone to the hanging breaking ball.
The Yankees have a 99 wRC+ as a team against right-handed pitching, and a 107 against lefties. Gray also took a no-hitter into the eighth inning against the Yankees back in late June, while Suárez was touched up in his last start against them.
What can be said either way is that having two accomplished veterans to follow the rookie gunslinger is a good position for the Red Sox to be in.

PHOENIX — Both the Yankees and Rays saw their respective games end in walk-off fashion on Saturday, but only one of the division rivals emerged victorious.
It wasn’t the Yanks, who suffered a 5-3 loss to the Diamondbacks when Michael Fulmer surrendered a game-ending, two-run home to Pavin Smith with one out in the ninth inning. Aaron Boone said that he considered using Clarke Schmidt, one game back from Tommy John surgery, instead, but he went with the journeyman Fulmer because he’s had more experience in those situations.
“I just felt like Fulmer’s been in these spots and throwing the ball really well for us, and Smith got him there,” Boone said of the reliever, who has a 3.09 ERA this season.
Meanwhile, at Tropicana Field, the Rays pulled off a 2-1 win over the Red Sox thanks to a bloop single from Richie Palacios in the ninth. Tampa now has a five-game lead over the Yankees with just eight games left in the regular season.
The American League East foes will play four of those games against each other at Yankee Stadium from Sept. 22-24, starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday. Boone acknowledged that his club will probably have to sweep the Rays for a crack at a division title.
“We sweep, then it gets interesting,” the manager said with the Yankees’ postseason ticket already punched.
But the odds are already stacked against the Yankees with the team finishing its series in Arizona on Sunday. They entered Saturday with a just a 2.8% chance of winning the division, according to FanGraphs.
Making matters tougher is that the Rays, owners of the AL’s best record, currently lead the season series between the two teams, 6-3. There’s also the fact that the Yankees will be without Aaron Judge, who returned to the injured list with calf strain on Saturday.
“They’re playing tremendous baseball, so it’s tough to climb up in the standings when they keep winning,” Cody Bellinger said after going 0-for-4 on Saturday. “So mathematically, it’s pretty tough, but gotta keep on rolling.”
“We gotta go on a good run. It’s gonna be tough,” added Cam Schlittler, who allowed one earned run over six innings but committed a costly error on Saturday. “I think we’ve had opportunities all season to put ourselves ahead, and we haven’t done a great job with it. So there’s still a chance, but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
The good news for the Yankees is that their best starters are lined up to face the Rays. While they haven’t officially announced their probables for the series, it looks like Max Fried and Carlos Rodón will pitch the doubleheader before Gerrit Cole and Schlittler, the Cy Young frontrunner, close out the four-game set.
The Rays, however, are set to throw a few of their best with Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez, Ian Seymour and Freddy Peralta slotted for the highly-anticipated matchup.
While they’re not officially out of the division race yet, the likeliest scenario is that the Yankees end up hosting Boston in the Wild Card round for the second straight year. It is not where the team wants to end up after finishing 2025 with the same record as the Blue Jays but losing the season series tiebreaker, but Bellinger remained confident that the Yankees can still win their first title since 2009.
“Obviously, the goal is to win the division, rest your guys, get those extra off days,” he said. “That’s always goal No. 1. Ultimately, World Series champions have come out of the Wild Card.”

Mike Thibault was with the Lakers during the early 1980s “Showtime” period, and he was with the Bulls when they drafted Michael Jordan. Then he moved around to different leagues, circumstances, and went back to the NBA as a Bucks assistant.
In 2003, he signed on to be the head coach the original Portland Fire of the WNBA, but Paul Allen, one of the richest men on earth, folded the franchise. Thibault learned the new Connecticut franchise wanted to talk to him, so he flew across the country, made the long drive in pitch darkness down Route 2 to find a shining city on hill.
“Then I look up and see the bright lights of the Mohegan Sun and the hotel and I thought, ‘Oh, this is different,'” Thibault said. “I stayed in the hotel the night before I was going to talk to them, and I went to the casino and won about $80, and the joke was, I told them, ‘well, if you don’t hire me, at least I got a little bit of your money.'”
All of Thibault’s quips landed and he became the first coach of the Connecticut Sun, leading them to the playoffs the first year, to the WNBA Finals in the second and third.
“It was pretty cool to be a part of that first non-NBA (affiliated) WNBA team,” he said, “having to fend for yourself without the backing of an NBA team in the market. I didn’t have trepidations about coaching women, I figured I would coach them just about the same way I coached men. I had been in the NBA, and then in the CBA, now the G League. I had never given much thought to coaching on the women’s side. But if I stayed in the NBA, I probably would have been a career assistant coach. I wanted to be a head coach. So I said, ‘why not?’ I was at a time in my life where if it wouldn’t be fatal (to my career) if it didn’t work out.”
The Sun made the playoffs in eight of their first 10 years, then let Thibault go after a loss in the conference finals in 2013. He went on to win the championship with Washington soon afterward, and he left The W as the winningest coach in its history, 379-289, though he has been passed by Cheryl Reeve. Now, as the Sun’s final season draws to a close, they will honor Mike Thibault during their second-to-last home game, the last name on the banner in the rafters of the arena noting those who were significant in the team’s history, a history both successful and yet oddly star-crossed.
“I was there 10 years and basically got fired in the midst of a good streak,” Thibault said, “and to be honored by the team, I don’t know that that usually happens in these situations. But I have such good memories of my time there. … The way the organization has handled a tough situation, with their “sunset season” theme, honoring former coaches and players, I think it’s very classy.”
Thibault, 75, now coaches Belgium’s national team, a commitment of 14-15 weeks per year, succeeding the final Sun coach, Rachid Meziane, in that position. Belgium finished fifth in the recent World Cup. Coaching in the WNBA in the summers gave Thibault a chance to settle in Connecticut and be around more for his son, Eric, now the coach of the Mystics, and his daughter, Carly Thibault-Dudonis, who is building an impressive legacy coaching Fairfield’s women. In The W, Mike Thibault was one of those who put a stamp on the league.
“Two teams folded that year, and one team moved to Connecticut,” he said. “But I knew the NBA’s commitment, and I knew David Stern’s commitment. so I didn’t worry about the WNBA not making it. Why not be a part of making something work? A lot of the coaches who came in at that time, Cheryl Reeve, Michael Cooper, Bill Laimbeer had a lasting impact. Before that, a lot of the coaches in the league were former college coaches and it was played more like the college game. The NBA influence brought a good blend, and it started to play more like a pro league.”
Today, he compares the league’s growth to the NBA in the 1980s, about 30 years into its history. “I think the game has gotten better, the talent is better, bigger, stronger, faster, better shooters, better athletes,” Thibault said. “It reminds me, I was in the NBA when it was about 30 years old and it started to take off during the 1980s with the talent level really high. The rules changes have allowed the game to be a little more free-flowing. It’s higher scoring, with the athlete taking over on the offensive side of the game. At times it gets physical, and it will be interesting to see how games are called during the playoffs. So TV is excited about it because it’s a more entertaining game.”
The Orlando franchise had been an underachiever, it was perceived. Thibault took over the roster in Connecticut and said his goal was to compete for the title, and he had Nykesha Sales and Rebecca Lobo for the chase.
“At my first press conference there were snickers when I said my first goal would be to play for a championship,” he said. “Everyone was like, ‘Dude!’ But you have to have that mindset going in. Then making the finals two years in a row. There were a lot of coulda, woulda, shoulda’s in both years. In 2006 I think we had our best team, but we were so injury-riddled and ground down when we got to the playoffs.”
In 2009, the Sun traded star Lindsay Whalen to the Lynx, a most painful moment for Thibault.
“I hated that I had to trade Lindsey Whalen,” Thibault said. “She was like a second daughter in my house. It was time because we couldn’t put enough players around her. But then we got Tina Charles and began the rebuild. We had the second youngest team in the league, the second lowest payroll, I was proud of that group. I got fired basically because I didn’t win a championship, even though we had committed two years earlier to the rebuild.”
Ultimately, Thibault jumped into a league struggling to survive and brought the credibility that helped stabilize a new franchise and the league — so in the larger picture he is more than just a “Sun Legend.” The Sun, purchased for $10 million in 2003, began making a profit in 2010, its location one of the reasons. Now it will go to Houston, having been sold for roughly $300 million.
The countdown is on for Sun’s final game in Connecticut is Sept. 24.
“I was sad,” Thibault said. “I understand it from a business standpoint, the league has changed, the money has changed. The salaries, the amenities you have to have, it’s hard to draw free agents, too. I felt bad for the fans more than anybody. … I thought Boston would have been a good compromise. The most disappointing thing was not winning a championship for our fans, the way they supported us. We gave it our best shot.”
More for your Sunday Read:
Filling iconic skates at UConn
Tia Chan was in goal for the UConn women’s hockey team for so long, playing at such a high level, one could almost call her an icon — rare for a college athlete. Now the Huskies, who reached the NCAA’s Elite Eight last year, have a strong cast of skaters led by high-scoring Claire Murdoch, but will be looking for the next goalie.
“We were worried when Elaine Chuli left (in 2016), we were worried when Morgan Fisher left (in 2020), we were worried when Annie Belanger left (2018),” coach Chris MacKenzie said. “I just think there is going to be someone who is going to step up. It’s happened enough over the 13 years we’ve been here, we’re going to need one of the three we have in there to step up.”
Senior Shannon Moran, freshman Ameilia Wilkinson and sophomore Taylor Belchetz are competing for the starting spot, and all three were expected to see action Saturday in the exhibition game vs. Quinnipiac, also an Elite Eight team, as was Yale.
Among the newcomers for MacKenzie are twin sisters Caileigh and Chelsea Tiller, who could have immediate impact as freshman. The UConn season begins at St. Cloud State Sept. 25.
Warnings from Wesleyan
Wesleyan football coach Dan DiCenso posted a video on social media this week in which he called out the New England Small School Athletic Conference for imposing roster limits on football.
“Football is the only sport in the NESAC with a mandated roster limit,” DiCenso begins. “If all the sports had a mandated roster limit and were making cuts, I would have no problem with it. So this week myself, and three or four schools in this situation, will cut kids from our team. This goes against all of Division III philosophy, all our NESCAC core values (to encourage participation in athletics).”
Wesleyan won the league title with no roster limits in 2024, and again when roster limits were put in for 2025, citing possible competitive advantages, capping at 84 players. DiCenso noted there are sports where there are large disparities between roster numbers.
“Common sense says, if there isn’t a roster limit in any other sport, why is there one in football?” he said. “… Do we want to talk about it? Or do we want to do something about it. I’m tired of having to meet with kids and not be able to give them a good reason why they can’t be on our team — just to practice and be there.”
Sunday short takes
*The Ivy League is moving its men’s basketball championship to Allentown, Pa., in 2028. Big mistake, I say. With the great, historic venues available in the league, most of which are easy for fans to reach, the Ivy’s four-team format was one of the most exciting and enjoyable of the conference tournaments. Messing with happy is never a good idea.
*Sports performance coaches should commission a study of the spotted lantern fly. Have you tried stepping on one? For a bug its size, it has to have the most explosive first step of any creature on earth.
*UConn men’s hockey coach Mike Cavanaugh filled out his staff with director of player development Ryan Shannon, Darien native, former Boston College and pro player and head coach at Taft School. Earlier, Sean Walsh, who also has pro playing experience, came from Alaska-Fairbanks to join Cavanaugh’s staff.
*Yard Goats manager Robinson Cancel will be a bench coach in the Mexican winter league with Tomateros de Culiacan. He will work with, and hopes to learn a lot from Lorenzo Bundy, a long-time MLB coach with a lot of pro managing experiencing.
*Jim Calhoun and his wife, Pat, will be honored by the University of Saint Joseph on Oct. 9 at the Connecticut Convention Center in Hartford. Tickets and details are available on USJ’s website at usj.edu/give/gala for: ‘A Legacy of Leadership. A Gala Honoring Pat and Jim Calhoun,’ the event to benefit the Calhoun Legacy Fund at USJ. Quite a few of Calhoun’s former players are expected.
*Art Shamsky, the 1969 Met, will be the guest at the Hartford World Series Club’s gathering on Sept. 23.
*Jackie Adams-Cheney, John Benoit, Dr. Kelly Harrigan, Robert Kalat, Sara Plourde-Zirkle, Tom Roberts, Don Sourcy and Jillian Sullivan are the Class of ’26 inductees for the Bristol Sports Hall of Fame. The induction ceremony will be Nov. 20 at the DoubleTree in Bristol, go to bshof.org for tickets and info.
*Dan Lauria, SCSU football player in the late 1960s, who turned to acting and gave us that quintessential 60s Dad on The Wonder Years, was inducted into the New Haven Gridiron Club Hall of Fame earlier this month.
Last word
*Cam Schlittler has been great for the Yankees, but any MVP talk is over the top. When starting pitchers threw complete games, they were viable candidates for both Cy Young and MVP, but it would be silly to give the MVP award to a five- or six-inning starter when there are sluggers like Yordan Alvarez flirting with the Triple Crown in Houston or Junior Caminero blowing past 40 homers for Tampa Bay.

There's a version of this continuous Boston Red Sox news saga that could have sent fans into a real panic, and I get why. Justin Slaten had quietly turned into one of the more trustworthy arms in this bullpen, working to a 2.84 ERA over his final two months of availability before elbow trouble sidelined him in August.
Now we know the full picture: an evaluation revealed degenerative changes in the flexor mass of his right elbow, and rather than push for a return with the postseason approaching, the Red Sox are having him get a PRP injection and start planning for 2027 instead.
On the year, he had thirty-six appearances, a 4.60 ERA overall, but provided a real chunk of high-leverage relief work, which is now gone for the stretch run. That's a real hole, absolutely. It's also not the whole story right now, and it's worth taking a breath before assuming the bullpen just got worse.
Garrett Crochet was the AL Cy Young runner-up last season, an 18-5, 2.59 ERA workhorse who threw 205.1 innings and struck out 255 batters. What a lot of people forget is that before all of that, Crochet broke into pro ball as a reliever with the Chicago White Sox, sitting comfortably in the upper 90s and regularly touching triple digits in short bursts. That's exactly the version the Red Sox may get back down the stretch.
He hasn't pitched in a game since throwing six scoreless innings on April 25, and after months sidelined with a shoulder issue that turned into more of a lingering problem, he just threw his first bullpen sessions in nearly three months. There isn't time left to stretch him back out as a starter, but a Crochet who can air it out for one to three innings at a time is exactly the profile that's thrived in October before.
Pair that with a Payton Tolle start going five or six innings, Crochet bridging the seventh and eighth, and Aroldis Chapman closing it out, and that's a real, dangerous alignment behind Sonny Gray in a Game 1.
Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo are trending toward returns to Red Sox bullpen alongside Garrett Crochet
Crochet isn't walking through that door alone, either. Tanner Houck is further along than anyone, working back from UCL surgery and already up to three innings and 48 pitches in a rehab outing for Double-A Portland, allowing just one run with four strikeouts, before moving on to Triple-A Worcester to keep building and facing some better competition.
Johan Oviedo, who Boston acquired from the Pittsburgh Pirates over the winter, finally made his own rehab appearance with Worcester this week after missing more than five months with a flexor strain, which is a sign he could factor into the bullpen picture before the year is out. Kutter Crawford is the longer shot of the group, hasn't pitched for the big club since 2024, and there are only unconfirmed "rumblings" he could get a look at Worcester this week. Even if that goes nowhere in 2026, he's still under team control for two more seasons.
Losing Slaten hurts, and nobody should pretend otherwise. But between Crochet, Houck, and Oviedo all trending in the right direction at the same time, Boston may be walking into the stretch run with more usable, high-upside arms than it's had healthy at any single point all season.

item.content:encoded:
El rol regular de la campaña 2026 de la MLB está por llegar a su final para darle paso a la postemporada, sin dejar de lado las atractivas distinciones individuales para los mejores peloteros del año.
Entre ellos, emerge la figura de Cam Schlittler, el estelar brazo de los New York Yankees que ha pasado de ser un novato en 2025, a ser el máximo candidato para el Cy Young de la Liga Americana este año, acorde con la herramienta de seguimiento de premios MLB de ESPN.
Sin embargo, Cam ahora apunta a una distinción de mayor categoría y los números lo están respaldando seriamente para meterse en la conversación por el MVP de la Liga Americana, y la herramienta de medición es ni más ni menos que Clayton Kershaw, el último pitcher, sea en el joven o en el viejo circuito, que ha obtenido el galardón en las Ligas Mayores.
Las cifras que acercan a Cam Schlittler al histórico MVP que ganó Clayton Kershaw
Este 2026, Cam Schlittler ha puesto números muy cercanos a los que le valieron a Kershaw para ser reconocido como el MVP de la Liga Nacional en 2014. Desde el zurdo que hizo historia con Los Ángeles Dodgers, ningún otro lanzador de tiempo completo ha obtenido el reconocimiento.
| Stat | Cam Schlittler 2026 | Clayton Kershaw 2014 |
|---|---|---|
| bWAR | 7.0 | 7.7 |
| ERA | 1.95 | 1.77 |
| ERA+ | 215 | 197 |
| K’s | 228 | 239 |
Estas cifras están presentadas antes de la apertura de Cam Schlittler de este mismo sábado 19 de septiembre frente a los Arizona Diamondbacks, y considerando que a los Yankees aún les restan series ante los Tampa Bay Rays y los Baltimore Orioles, lo más probable es que el franela #31 de los ‘Mulos’ todavía tenga otra salida antes de la conclusión del rol regular de la campaña.
¿Puede realmente Schlittler ganar el MVP de la Liga Americana?
Aunque los números han sido espectaculares para el derecho de 25 años, la propia herramienta de seguimiento de premios MLB de ESPN indica que, en este momento, el favorito para ser reconocido como el jugador más valioso del joven circuito es, con buena diferencia, Yordan Álvarez.
Y no es para menos, el designado de los Houston Astros batea en este 2026 para .312, con un OPS de 1.031, ha pegado 40 palos de vuelta entera, habiendo anotado 98 carreras e impusaldo 99. Cifras hasta antes del segundo juego de la serie de los ‘Space Boys’ ante los Atlanta Braves de este sábado.
Un candidato muy sólido como para que Cam Schlittler aspire a ser reconocido con el MVP, considerando que en el listado de candidatos también aparece otro bate de peso como Junior Caminero, su rival divisional de los Tampa Bay Rays.
Pitchers que han ganado el MVP en MLB
- Clayton Kershaw - Los Ángeles Dodgers | 2014
- Justin Verlander - Detroit Tigres | 2011
- Dennis Eckersley - Oakland Athletics | 1992
- Roger Clemens - Boston Red Sox | 1986
- Willie Hernández - Detroit Tigers | 1984
- Rollie Fingers - Milwaukee Brewers | 1981
- Vida Blue - Oakland Athletics | 1971
- Denny McLain - Detroit Tigers | 1968
- Bob Gibson - St. Louis Cardinals | 1968

The 2026 season could end up being Sonny Gray’s last.
The veteran right-hander, who turns 37 in November, has not committed to pitching in 2027 and recently told The Boston Globe he would retire “in a heartbeat” if his family wanted him to do so.
Boston reportedly is taking the possibility seriously, according to the outlet, with some in the organization believing retirement is on the table despite Gray’s strong season.
Asked recently about the possibility of retirement, Gray declined to say much.
“We can get into that at another time but not right now,” he said, per the Globe.
If 2026 is, indeed, his final big league season, Gray’s final start could come in the increasingly likely matchup against the rival Yankees during the wild-card round of the postseason.
Gray spent a season and a half in pinstripes after coming over before the 2017 trade deadline, and it didn’t go exactly as planned for either him or the team.
The three-time All-Star posted a 4.51 ERA across 41 games (34 starts) with the Yankees before being traded to Cincinnati before the 2019 season, during which he posted a Cy Young-caliber season with the Reds.
Gray ripped the Yankees during his introductory press conference with the Red Sox over the winter.
“It feels good to me to go to a place where it’s easy to hate the Yankees,” Gray said.
“I never wanted to go there in the first place.”
Gray is enjoying one of the best seasons of his 14-year MLB career in Beantown, posting a 2.82 ERA in 163 innings.
“I’ve very, very much so enjoyed Boston. Enjoyed the guys. Fenway has been, and is, a very special place,” Gray said.

PHOENIX — Cam Schlittler llega este sábado al Chase Field con otra oportunidad de convertir una temporada que ya es dominante en algo aún más difícil de alcanzar para el resto de la Liga Americana.
El lanzador diestro de los Yankees llega a su partido contra Arizona con un balance de 14-6, una efectividad de 1,95, un WHIP de 0,90 y 228 strikeouts en 184 2/3 entradas. Ha cedido una carrera o menos en siete salidas seguidas, una racha que le ha llevado de ser un simple aspirante a situarse en el centro de las conversaciones sobre el premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, mientras que los Yankees se han asegurado otra plaza en la postemporada.
El contraste con su rival más cercano se acentuó el viernes por la noche sin que Schlittler lanzara ni una sola bola. El as de Toronto, Dylan Cease , solo aguantó 2 2/3 entradas en la derrota por 7-1 ante Texas. Concedió seis bases por bolas, encajó cuatro carreras (solo una limpia) y solo 36 de sus 74 lanzamientos fueron strikes. Sportsnet también midió su bola rápida a 93,6 mph, 3,3 mph por debajo de su media de la temporada.
Cease sigue teniendo una temporada de élite. Tras la derrota, tiene un balance de 11-6, con una ERA de 2,40, un WHIP de 1,10 y 239 strikeouts en 169 entradas, lo que le sitúa a la cabeza de la Liga Americana. Su total de ponches sigue siendo mejor que el de Schlittler. Sin embargo, su promedio de carreras limpias, la eficiencia en su carga de trabajo y su control reciente marcan ahora un contraste estadístico más marcado, justo en el momento en que las opiniones sobre los premios se van consolidando.
Para los Yankees, eso va más allá de los trofeos. Schlittler se ha convertido en el miembro más estable de un cuerpo de lanzadores de los Yankees que ha tenido que lidiar con las ausencias de Gerrit Cole, Max Fried y Carlos Rodón. Además, está previsto que sea el primero en lanzar en la rotación de Nueva York en octubre, lo que hace que sus últimas salidas en la temporada regular cobren importancia tanto para la lucha por los playoffs como para la carrera por los premios.
Los Yankees llegan al sábado con un balance de 89-64, a cuatro partidos de Tampa Bay, así que cada salida que le queda sigue teniendo un interés inmediato más allá de la carrera por los premios.
Una votación unánime cambia el panorama de la carrera
Esta semana ha llegado la señal más clara hasta ahora. En la última votación del premio Cy Young de la temporada en MLB.com, los 32 votantes eligieron al as de los Yankees como el número uno de la Liga Americana. Consiguió el máximo de 160 puntos. Cease quedó segundo con 126.
El jurado pidió a los votantes que clasificaran a cinco lanzadores en una escala del 5 al 1 (5-4-3-2-1), teniendo en cuenta tanto lo que había pasado como cómo podrían desarrollarse las dos últimas semanas. Esa distinción es importante. La encuesta no es la votación oficial de la BBWAA y no decide el premio, pero la unanimidad entre los 32 votantes de MLB.com muestra lo mucho que ha subido la posición del as de los Yankees.
El último modelo de premios de ESPN apunta en la misma dirección. Su sistema AXE sitúa a Schlittler en primer lugar entre los lanzadores de la Liga Americana con 153,1, por delante de Cease, que tiene 145,8. ESPN señaló que Schlittler ya llevaba un balance de 12-6 con una efectividad de 2,09 hasta agosto, y que luego empezó septiembre con un 2-0 y una efectividad de 0,89 en sus tres primeras salidas del mes.
El caso de Cone explica por qué los números tienen más peso
David Cone ha definido el valor de Schlittler basándose en algo más sencillo que una fórmula para los premios. El exganador del premio Cy Young de los Yankees destacó la constancia con la que este lanzador diestro ha aliviado la presión de anotar sobre la alineación y el bullpen.
«¿Dónde estarían los Yankees sin él?», dijo Cone.
A continuación, Cone situó a Schlittler al mismo nivel que las estrellas más valiosas de la liga al hablar de lo mucho que Nueva York ha dependido de él a lo largo de una temporada marcada por los cambios constantes en la rotación.
«Schlittler está entre los mejores. Se lo merece, sin duda hay que tenerlo muy en cuenta», dijo Cone.
Ese argumento viene respaldado por la trayectoria de Schlittler esta temporada. Cone señaló esta semana que el lanzador diestro ya había hecho 21 salidas en las que solo había cedido cero o una carrera. En las últimas siete salidas de Schlittler, las estadísticas actuales de la MLB muestran una efectividad de 1,00 en 45 entradas, con 57 ponches y un WHIP de 0,76.
El tropiezo de Cease marca la diferencia en los últimos compases
Lo más revelador es el momento en que se hizo la encuesta. La encuesta de MLB.com se publicó antes de la salida más corta de Cease esta temporada, el viernes en Arlington. Eso significa que el resultado unánime no necesitó su último tropiezo para diferenciar a los dos lanzadores.
Las estadísticas de Cease siguen siendo lo suficientemente buenas como para que la carrera siga siendo reñida. Tiene 11 strikeouts más que Schlittler en 15 2/3 entradas menos. Pero también ha concedido 78 bases por bolas frente a las 44 de Schlittler, y el viernes fue la tercera salida consecutiva en la que Cease no logró completar seis entradas.
Schlittler tendrá la próxima oportunidad de demostrar su valía. Los Yankees lo alinearán contra Brandon Pfaadt el sábado, con Nueva York con un balance de 89-64, a cuatro partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana y con la clasificación para la postemporada ya asegurada. Una buena actuación no garantizaría oficialmente el premio, pero dejaría aún menos margen para que algún rival cambie el panorama de esta recta final de la temporada.
Queda una última prueba antes de octubre
A los Yankees aún les queda más de una semana antes de que termine la temporada regular, y los aficionados de los Yankees saben que las votaciones para los premios no se basan en encuestas de predicción. Una o dos malas salidas finales aún pueden cambiar el panorama. Esa es la incertidumbre que Schlittler debe afrontar.
Lo que ha cambiado es la carga de la prueba. Schlittler ya no tiene que esforzarse por meterse en la conversación. Las últimas medidas a nivel nacional ya lo han situado al frente, mientras que el mal viernes de Cease ha hecho que la carrera sea aún más dura.
El sábado en Arizona le da al as de los Yankees otra oportunidad de ampliar aún más esa ventaja.

item.content:encoded:
In the absence of Shohei Ohtani and Aaron Judge, the mysterious power outages of Vlad Guerrero Jr. and Cal Raleigh, and the injuries to Tarik Skubal and Garrett Crochet, baseball’s postseason awards are coming into focus by ushering in a new wave of 20-something superstars.
Going into the weekend the teams with the best records in each league were the small market Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays, both of which with leading candidates for baseball’s postseason hardware who are still years away from their prime.
For the Brewers, 24-year-old Jacob Misiorowski is the runaway leader for the NL Cy Young Award, at 15-5 and leading the majors in ERA (1.89), strikeouts (243), WHIP (0.812) and strikeouts per nine innings (13.1) — while the Rays, in their bid to salt away the AL East, have gotten a late boost from their 23-year old third baseman Junior Caminero, who took over the AL home run lead last week and was neck and neck with Houston’s Yordan Alvarez in RBI and total bases.
On the surface, Alvarez, who leads the NL in OPS and batting (.311), would appear to have the overall statistical edge on Caminero for the MVP. But the fact that Alvarez is a DH and Caminero, who’s missed only one game while adding superior defense at third base for a team that is likely to win the division also bodes well for him. This is one race that figures to go down to the last day, with the deciding factor possibly being whether the Astros win the AL West.
As for the AL Cy Young Award, Cam Schlittler, the Yankees’ 25-year-old sophomore, has zoomed ahead of the Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease with a season for the ages, including a major league-leading 1.95 ERA and 0.904 WHIP and the most starts in Yankee history allowing one or fewer runs (21). His 1.14 ERA for 16 road starts is also the lowest in American League history.
Over in the National League, with Ohtani shackled with knee and bicep injuries that have prevented him from pitching since July 3, effectively ending his chances for a fourth straight MVP, the Cubs’ 24-year-old Pete Crow-Armstrong has stepped up with a phenomenal breakthrough season. Going into the weekend, Crow-Armstrong, who’s played every game, was leading the majors in slugging, OPS and total bases and was second behind Kyle Schwarber in the NL in homers with 44 and third in RBI with 105. On Aug. 29 he hit three homers in a game and with his 44th homer on Sept. 17 surpassed Hall of Famer Billy Williams as the most by a left-handed hitter in Cubs history.
Sorry, but we’re again unable to refrain from reminding that Crow-Armstrong was the Mets’ 2020 first round draft pick who, the next season, they traded to the Cubs for two months of rental free agent Javy Baez.
When it comes to the Rookies of the Year, I realize in this lost season for the Mets there’s been a lot of buzz for Nolan McLean and Carson Benge, but neither are going to win the NL award. That would have to be Cincinnati’s unsung Sal Stewart, who even if nobody probably had him on their Rookie of the Year bingo card at the start of the season, happens to be leading all NL rookies in homers (32) and RBI (110) and has played every day. An equally strong favorite for the AL Rookie of the Year is Cleveland lefty Parker Messick, a second round draft pick out of Florida State three years ago, who leads all AL rookies in wins (12), ERA (2.57), strikeouts (186) and WHIP (1.04).
IT’S A MADD, MADD WORLD
You have to wonder if the window has already closed on Aaron Judge leading the Yankees to a World Series title. The 34-year-old Yankee captain has missed 317 games (and counting) and had only four full seasons since 2018 and the fact remains he’s 280 pounds — and every time he has to make a diving catch or crash into a wall at his age now that’s 280 pounds of impact on his body. No surprise the rib injury that’s sidelined him most of this season. … For nine decades, Juan Vene was a fixture in the press boxes of Yankee Stadium and Shea Stadium and even though his name may not be familiar to most New York baseball fans, he was a legend, especially in his native Venezuela, but really all over Latin America. Word came last week that Vene passed away Sept. 15 in Miami at age 97. A long-time member of the Baseball Writers Association and a regular Hall of Fame voter, Vene was a friend to all of us. Anyone needing an interview with a Latin player in the offseason could count on Vene to help set it up. RIP. … If the White Sox are somehow able to hold on and win the AL Central it will be a remarkable achievement given the year-long state of their starting pitching. According to the Elias Bureau, White Sox starters have logged by far the fewest innings (639) in the majors to the runner-up Nationals’ 671 1/3, and as they stagger to the finish line they have been employing “openers” 2-3 times a week.

La temporada 2026 de las Grandes Ligas entra en su tramo definitivo y la carrera por el Cy Young de la Liga Nacional comienza a tomar forma. Mientras algunos lanzadores todavía buscan cerrar fuerte para meterse en la conversación, Jacob Misiorowski ha conseguido separarse del resto gracias a una campaña en la que ha mostrado un nivel sobresaliente con los Milwaukee Brewers.
¿Por qué Jacob Misiorowski es el favorito al Cy Young?
Misiorowski ha sido particularmente consistente durante 2026 y encabeza a los pitchers abridores de MLB en varias categorías relevantes. Su dominio incluso se ha mantenido durante el último tramo de la campaña, una situación que ha fortalecido sus argumentos de cara al premio.
Durante agosto, el lanzador de los Brewers registró una efectividad de 2.32, cifra que representó su segundo peor registro mensual de toda la temporada. Su peor mes fue abril, cuando terminó con 3.58 de efectividad, lo que refleja la regularidad que ha mantenido conforme avanzó el calendario.
Uno de los lanzadores que todavía puede competir por el reconocimiento es Cristopher Sánchez, de los Philadelphia Phillies. El zurdo fue considerado uno de los principales favoritos al inicio de la carrera después de encadenar 50 entradas y dos tercios sin permitir carrera entre finales de abril y principios de junio. Aunque posteriormente perdió algo de terreno, sus números lo mantienen como un contendiente relevante.
Sánchez, de 29 años, lidera MLB en victorias con una marca de 16-4 y además presume una efectividad de 2.52, WHIP de 1.19 y 202 ponches en 175.1 entradas. Su desempeño lo mantiene dentro de la conversación, aunque ahora deberá aprovechar las últimas semanas de la temporada para intentar recortar distancia.
Otro nombre que aparece entre los contendientes es Chris Sale, de los Atlanta Braves. El veterano zurdo cuenta con experiencia y argumentos suficientes para mantenerse en la disputa, aunque Misiorowski ha conseguido colocarse por delante del grupo gracias al dominio mostrado a lo largo de la campaña.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto, el caballo negro
Yoshinobu Yamamoto representa una alternativa que no puede descartarse. El japonés se ha convertido en una pieza constante de la rotación de los Los Angeles Dodgers y sus números reflejan el nivel que ha alcanzado durante su segunda temporada en las Grandes Ligas.
Después de 24 aperturas, Yamamoto tiene marca de 12-8, efectividad de 2.56 y un espectacular WHIP de 0.89. Además, suma 153 ponches y únicamente 36 bases por bolas en 158 entradas de trabajo. Son estadísticas que en otras temporadas podrían colocarlo directamente entre los favoritos.

item.content:encoded:
By any objective measure, Cam Schlittler, in his first full season in the majors, is having one of the best seasons any Yankees starter has ever had.
Schlittler, who is expected to start Saturday against the Diamondbacks in Phoenix, is 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA. Those numbers alone, however, don’t tell the full story of Schlittler’s 2026 season, one that has established him as a co-favorite, along with Dylan Cease of the Blue Jays, for the American League Cy Young Award.
After Schlittler threw six scoreless innings Sunday afternoon in a 2-0 victory over the Mets, manager Aaron Boone even made a push for him to be considered for another award.
“He might be the MVP, too,” Boone said. “It’s been awesome. Just an awesome season.”
That, of course, is a long shot at best. Many voters, not to mention players, see the MVP as the sole dominion of position players, just as the Cy Young Award is reserved for pitchers.
“He’s definitely pitching like an MVP,” Aaron Judge said after Sunday's win. “They’ve got a Cy Young Award for a reason — best pitcher in the game. He’s got my vote definitely for the Cy Young.”
Regardless, Schlittler is in the midst of a strong finishing kick to his year, and it is not a stretch to say he has emerged as the favorite with just over a week left in the regular season.
Though Schlittler has the edge over Cease in many of the numbers — traditional as well as what would be considered more “modern” ones — used when it comes to evaluating pitchers for the Cy Young Award, Cease has some of those in his favor as well.
Digging into many of those numbers, all of them as of Wednesday afternoon:
Schlittler is second in the American League in wins with 14 compared to 11 for Cease (11-6), though Cy Young Award voters have put little emphasis on wins in the last decade-plus.
The Mariners' Felix Hernandez, for instance, won the AL Cy Young Award in 2010 after going 13-12 (with an MLB-leading 2.27 ERA, one of many statistics, both old-school and new-school, in which he led). The Mets' Jacob deGrom won the NL award in 2018 after going 10-9 (with an MLB-best 1.70 ERA and dominating pretty much every other statistical category), and the Pirates' Paul Skenes took NL honors last season after going 10-10 (with an MLB-leading 1.97 ERA and widespread statistical dominance elsewhere).
Cease pitched against the Rangers on Friday night. Entering that game, Schlittler led him in ERA, 1.95 to 2.38; walks and hits per innings pitched (WHIP), 0.90 to 1.06; innings, 184 2/3 to 166 1/3, and Wins above Replacement, 7.0 to 6.1, according to baseball-reference.com, and 5.9 to 5.6, according to Fangraphs.com.
Schlittler also held the edge in ERA+, a statistic measuring the quality of a pitcher’s ERA compared to the league average, adjusting to the ballpark he pitches in, with the league average being 100.
Cease’s ERA+ was 185, a terrific, Cy Young Award-worthy number in many years, but this year it ranked him second in the AL to Schlittler’s extraordinary ERA+ of 216 (deGrom’s ERA+ in 2018 was 218, Skenes’ in 2025 was 226).
Schlittler's “calling card” from the time he was promoted to the big leagues in July 2025 has been command, according to Boone, and he dominates Cease in that category as well.
Despite pitching 18 1/3 more innings, Schlittler has walked only 44 batters to Cease's 72. Schlittler ranks fifth in the AL in walks per nine innings at 2.1 and Cease ranks 22nd at 3.9.
Cease does have some numbers in his favor.
Despite throwing 18 1/3 fewer innings, Cease had 236 strikeouts, tied for the MLB lead, to Schlittler’s 228, giving the former a ratio of 12.8 strikeouts per nine innings to the latter’s 11.1. Cease had 13 games with at least nine strikeouts, the most of any pitcher in the AL, and Schlittler has seven such games.
Cease has been slightly harder to hit, with opposing batters producing a .177 batting average against, which leads the AL among qualified starting pitchers, compared to a .185 batting average against for Schlittler (which ranks him second in that category). Entering Friday, Cease was allowing 5.7 hits per nine innings and Schlittler is allowing 6.0.
Cease had allowed only 11 homers in his 166 1/3 innings and Schlittler has allowed 16 in his 184 2/3 innings.
Cease also holds the edge over Schlittler in Fielding Independent Pitching (FIP), which attempts to measure a pitcher’s performance based on those elements he directly controls before a ball is put in play and the vagaries of defense become a factor. Those would be strikeouts, walks, homers allowed and hit batsmen.
Cease led the AL in FIP at 2.48. Schlittler is second at 2.57.
Though Cease does hold an advantage in some of the difficulty-to-hit categories, they likely won’t be enough — at the moment, anyway — to deny Schlittler's bid to become the seventh Yankee to win a Cy Young Award (Gerrit Cole was the most recent in 2023).
And there’s this: Schlittler’s closing argument has been especially eye-popping. He’s allowed one run or fewer in an MLB-leading (and franchise-record) 21 starts this season, including in each of his last seven starts, going 4-0 with a 1.00 ERA and a 0.76 WHIP in that span. He has a 0.81 ERA and 0.72 WHIP in those 21 games. In two other games, he allowed zero or one earned run.
Schlittler has allowed three or fewer runs in 27 of his 31 starts and two or fewer in 24 of them.
Cease had 16 outings in which he allowed one run or fewer, certainly an impressive number, but had not pitched quite as well of late, 4-0 with a 2.70 ERA in his previous seven outings.

RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses starter Sonny Gray joining Red Sox Hall of Famer Tim Wakefield in franchise history. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
The Boston Red Sox avoided a sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers on Thursday night thanks to a 4-3 win that was powered by an eighth-inning, go-ahead, three-run home run off the bat of shortstop Trevor Story. While Story's big swing was undoubtedly the story of the game, Boston was in position to win because of Sonny Gray's fantastic start, a start that saw him join Red Sox Hall of Famer Tim Wakefield in the history books.
Gray tossed 6.1 innings, allowing just three earned runs on three hits while striking out six and walking three. According to Red Sox Nation Stats on Twitter/X, Gray became the first pitcher aged 36 or older to log 21 or more starts of six or more innings pitched since Wakefield did so in 2008.
Gray has been nothing short of a revelation since arriving in Boston on an offseason deal with the St. Louis Cardinals. The 36-year-old veteran was brought in, in part, to be the "Robin" to Garrett Crochet's "Batman." However, because of the shoulder injury that has kept Crochet out of the rotation since late April, Gray has served as "Batman" just as well as the 2025 American League Cy Young Award runner-up could have.
In Crochet's absence, Gray has posted a 2.57 ERA in 23 starts, spanning 140 innings pitched. The team has gone 17-6 in those starts. Not only has Gray been Boston's best starter since the Crochet injury, but he's also been one of the best arms in baseball in the stretch, with his ERA ranking as the sixth-lowest mark over that time.
Overall, Gray has posted a 2.82 ERA that ranks fifth best among all American League starters, doing it in 163 innings with an fWAR of 3.2 that sits just outside the top 10 at No. 11. Perhaps most importantly, even when the 36-year-old veteran doesn't have his best stuff, he keeps the team in a position to win, as was evident on Thursday night.
When Gray was first acquired, many questioned whether he could still be a top of the rotation arm. Now, after answering those questions with a season that'll likely see him finish top five in American League Cy Young Award voting, the only question that remains is whether he'll return for 2027 and beyond.
Up next for the Sox
After dropping two of three in Texas, the Red Sox' final regular-season road trip rolls on as they open a three-game series at Tropicana Field against the likely American League East champion Tampa Bay Rays on Friday night. Ranger Suarez (7-4, 3.33 ERA) gets the start for Boston opposite Ian Seymour (9-6, 4.27 ERA) for Tampa Bay. First pitch is set for 7:10 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox starting pitcher Sonny Gray has been one of the best hurlers in baseball this season, entering the weekend in the mix to win the American League Cy Young Award. While he’ll likely be pitching in October for Boston, keeping him long-term reportedly could be an issue.
MassLive.com‘s Chris Cotillo reports that Gray could command a three-year contract this winter, potentially in the range of $75 million total. It would be closely aligned to what Nathan Eovaldi received in December 2024 with the Texas Rangers.
The project salary for Gray is fairly reasonable given how well he’s performed on the mound this season. At a $25 million average annual value, he would be tied for 17th among the highest-paid starting pitchers in MLB.
Given the financial flexibility that Boston has, it should be a reasonable price to tack onto the Red Sox payroll in 2027. However, Cotillo also wrote that Gray disclosed in an interview with The Boston Globe that the 36-year-old will retire “in a heartbeat” if his family wants him to step away from baseball and be around them more.
Gray will turn 37 years old in November and he’s already pulled in more than $125 million in career MLB earnings, according to Spotrac.com. The Tennessee native has a home in Nashville, where his wife and their two children reside. He’s reportedly spent his off days visiting them and, per Cotillo, the Red Sox organization believes retirement is a real possibility.
If Gray retires, that creates an immediate void in the Red Sox rotation ahead of an MLB free agency class that is not particularly deep when it comes to proven starting pitchers. Assuming Tarik Skubal is outside of Boston’s price range, Trevor Rogers and Freddy Peralta are the top options expected to be available.

The Boston Red Sox starter is working his way back from a right elbow injury.
Video Transcript
What's up, everyone?
Zach Coe here for Roundtable.
Ahead of Tuesday night's loss to the Rangers, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters that reliever Justin Slayton's season was over after an orthopedic visit revealed degenerative changes in his flexor mass, which required a PRP injection, effectively ending his season.
So obviously, the Red Sox have one of the best bullpens in baseball, backend of Aroldis Chapman, Justin Slayton, and Tayron Guerrero when he returns from the injured list.
But the loss of Slayton is still a really big one for this Red Sox bullpen, especially in the postseason when managers tend to be more aggressive with the hooks on both starters and relievers.
It was a pretty underwhelming season for Slayton when you look at the final line.
It was a 4.60 ERA in 31 1/3 innings.
But he was prone to a couple blowup starts, and that really inflated his ERA for much of the season.
It'll be interesting to see how Tracy's able to piece together the bullpen in Slayton's absence.
Of course, like I said, you have the backend pretty solidified with Tayron Guerrero handling the seventh, Garrett Whitlock in the eighth to All-Star Aroldis Chapman, who's been one of the best closers in baseball over the last two seasons.
But it's how you get to them that I really have some concerns about, and there are plenty of guys that are available to fill that role, but it's whether or not they'll be able to capitalize on their opportunities.
First one being Greg Weiser.
I wrote about it a little bit earlier, but ever since he was recalled from his brief demotion to Triple-A, he's been incredible for the Red Sox, stepping up as they lost guys like Whitlock to an IL stint, Slayton, who landed on the IL shortly after Whitlock, and most recently Guerrero.
There's also Tanner Houk, who's working his way back from Tommy John surgery he underwent last year.
He's gonna try to make a return in a bullpen capacity for the last week of the season.
And then there's the big wild card of it all in Garrett Crochet, who continues to throw side sessions as he tries to get back in a relief role for the postseason.
He's been on the injured list since April 29th with left shoulder inflammation.
So any of those guys are more than capable of stepping up and filling that role.
It's just gonna be about whether or not they're, one, healthy enough to go out there and throw on a near nightly basis like the team might need them to in the postseason, and two, whether or not they're gonna be productive enough.
Obviously, with Houk, he's coming back from Tommy John surgery, and typically you see guys be a little bit wild with their control when they first come back from Tommy John.
We saw it in Houk's first relea-- We saw it in his first rehab appearance with Portland.
He walked two guys, and a run scored as a result.
But it's been a little bit better, since then in the two appearances following that.
So we'll see if that is something that he can shake.
And then Crochet, he's just We haven't seen him in so long, it's tough to say whether or not he's gonna be as effective as he once was.
And even if he isn't able to get to the 2025 Cy Young runner-up caliber, can he at least give you enough to kind of bridge that gap between the starter and to the backend of your bullpen?
And then there's kind of a wild card in it all, and a bit of a forgotten man in Johan Oviedo, who obviously has electric stuff, but he's made only one appearance in a Red Sox uniform before landing on the IL with right elbow inflammation.
So he's planning on making a rehab appearance with Triple-A Worcester on Thursday night, and then they'll figure out the next steps with him.
But Red Sox have plenty of options to fill that void left behind by Slayton.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox made one of the very best moves in baseball for the 2026 season, despite the fact that some fans didn't initially believe in the deal.
While searching for a No. 2 starter last offseason, Boston turned to the St. Louis Cardinals and swung a deal for three-time All-Star Sonny Gray. With the Red Sox searching for another elite starter, some wondered if Gray was better suited for a mid-to-back of the rotation spot, rather than the No. 2 spot for a club with World Series aspirations. He has more than delivered and has been Boston's best starter all season. Gray's going to get Cy Young Award votes and Boston should do what it can to try to keep him in town beyond the 2026 season. If he plays, he'll cost a pretty penny. MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo reported that some in the industry believe Gray will get a deal in the range of three years and $75 million — or more — if he continues his career.
"As a free agent, Gray’s renaissance season may position him to receive a lucrative deal that some in the industry expect to match or exceed the three-year, $75 million deal the Rangers gave to Nathan Eovaldi two winters ago," Cotillo wrote. "Interestingly, though, Gray has not committed to pitching again in 2027. In a recent interview with The Boston Globe, Gray said he would retire 'in a heartbeat' if his family signaled that he was wanted back home year-round, even if that meant retiring after the end of this year."
The Red Sox Should Do Everything To Keep Sonny Gray
That's actually also the same deal that the Cardinals gave Gray before the 2024 season as well. He inked a three-year, $75 million pact that he's currently in the final year of. After the season, Gray has a $30 million mutual option for the 2027 season with a $10 million buyout. If Boston picks up its end of the buyout and Gray opts out, then the buyout would be forfeited.
Gray has pitched well enough in a Red Sox uniform to get paid again — if he keeps pitching. So far this season, he has a 17-5 record, 2.76 ERA and 4.0 wins above replacement in 156 2/3 innings pitched. When it comes to Gray, his age stands out at 36 years old. But it hasn't stopped him yet. The price of pitching has gone up in a big way. A deal with a $25 million annual value, as Cotillo pointed out, would be in the range of guys like Michael King, Sean Manaea, and Eovaldi. It would be just above guys like Aaron Nola, Seth Lugo, Robbie Ray and Luis Severino. Gray has been better than all of these guys so far this season.
When it comes to the Red Sox, there isn't as much pitching depth down in the minors as there once was. Over the last year, Boston has traded guys like Hunter Dobbins, Richard Fitts, Brandon Clarke, Anthony Eyanson and Kyson Witherspoon, among others. Plus, Connelly Early was traded as well.
Garrett Crochet, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suárez, and Jake Bennett are locks for the 2027 rotation. Johan Oviedo is someone who could play a role. Tanner Houck is another guy who could as well. We've seen all season how impactful injuries are to the rotation. You never have enough arms. A dependable veteran like Gray for the next few years should be a necessity. It's no guarantee that he pitches beyond the 2026 season, but if he does, it should be in a Boston uniform.

We won't spend too long belaboring how bad the Kyle Harrison-Caleb Durbin looked for the Boston Red Sox after a few months; the southpaw had emerged as a genuine National League Cy Young contender for the Milwaukee Brewers in the first half, while the third baseman was one of the league's worst qualified hitters through the beginning of June. Tack on the fact that Shane Drohan has become a valuable starter in his own right this year while Andruw Monasterio has been worth negative fWAR, and you've got a recipe for an all-time disaster of a trade.
And yet, after the tide began shifting over the summer, we can now definitively say the pendulum has swung back in the other direction. Durbin has been a star since June 1, posting an .812 OPS and a 129 wRC+. Meanwhile, Harrison is struggling so badly that he's now been moved out of the Brewers' rotation entirely.
It's far too early to suggest that the Red Sox have made up that early gap and are now the winners of the blockbuster trade, but it's clear that their decision to go all-in for Durbin wasn't a foolish one.
Red Sox just need to break even now to win Caleb Durbin trade in the future
In that same post-June-1 span, Harrison has pitched to an 6.10 ERA and 5.38 FIP, allowing a whopping 17 home runs over just 59 innings. A bout with forearm tightness near the All-Star break definitely has something to do with his second-half collapse, but he hasn't been pitching like an ace for quite a while. The fact that there's been conversations about him being left off the Brewers' postseason roster entirely should tell you all you need to know about the southpaw's recent struggles.
Durbin is trending in the exact opposite direction, as he's currently the seventh-most valuable third baseman in the league by fWAR (2.9) this season. A lot of that has to do with how excellent his baserunning and glove have been, but saying that someone is above average in every phase of the game isn't exactly a bad thing. He's a couple of steals and some favorable votes away from a 20 SB, Gold Glove campaign in his Red Sox debut. Not too shabby, eh?
It's also worth factoring in the other players Craig Breslow pried out of Milwaukee; neither Monasterio nor Anthony Seigler have been great in limited duty in Boston, but the former has produced some timely hits while playing all four infield positions while the latter has a 102 wRC+ in just under 175 plate appearances this year.
Then there's Owen Hull, whom the Red Sox selected with the compensatory draft pick the Brewers forked over in the trade. All he did after being drafted was mash in High-A, posting a .967 OPS in 24 games.
With Durbin under contract through 2031 and Hull sure to fly up the prospect rankings over the offseason, there's a good chance that the Sox can win this trade down the road, so long as they continue to break even for now.

RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the potential relievers who could step up and fill the void left behind by Justin Slaten after it was revealed the right-hander was unlikely to return from the injured list in 2026. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
After an incredible July that saw the Boston Red Sox go 21-4, ultimately saving their season and propelling them into postseason position, the team has given key contributors time on the injured list to address lingering injuries. Among the players placed on the IL was right-handed reliever Justin Slaten, who was dealing with right elbow soreness.
After initially expecting to miss the minimum of 15 days or somewhere close to it, the 29-year-old continued to experience soreness as he began throwing progressions, leading the team to shut him down each time. On Tuesday, interim manager Chad Tracy announced that Slaten received a PRP injection to treat "degenerative changes in his flexor mass," ending his season.
With Slaten set to miss the remainder of the year, the pressure is on these pitchers to help bridge the gap between the starter and All-Star closer Aroldis Chapman:
Tyron Guerrero
Guerrero was expected to be activated off the injured list ahead of Wednesday night's loss to the Texas Rangers, but tightness in his lower back led the team to delay his activation. Still, though, upon his activation, Guerrero will become one of the primary seventh-inning options for Tracy to turn to.
The 35-year-old flamethrower has been an incredible find for Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow, posting a 3.26 ERA in 38.2 innings in 2026. However, he hit a rough patch before landing on the IL, allowing eight earned runs in his last 13.2 innings. Boston will need him to return to the pitcher he was for the first 38.2 innings of his season, when he posted a 2.16 ERA.
After not allowing a single earned run in his first 10 appearances after being dealt to Boston at the trade deadline, the 28-year-old lefty has struggled in his last six outings, allowing five earned runs, including three in a blow-up appearance in Wednesday's loss.
Miller told reporters after the loss that he was working through a mechanical issue that led to the struggles. However, he is the primary left-handed high-leverage arm before Chapman, so the team will need him to get those issues squared away ahead of what's likely to be a Wild Card-round matchup against a New York Yankees lineup that's lefty-heavy.
No single pitcher has stepped up more for the Red Sox as they shuffled Garrett Whitlock, Slaten, and Guerrero on the injured list than Weissert. After a brief demotion to Triple-A Worcester on Aug. 7, Weissert returned to the big leagues on Aug. 13, taking Whitlock's spot on the active roster, and has been lights out ever since. In 10.2 innings since being recalled, the 31-year-old right-hander has allowed only two earned runs on 12 hits, striking out 14 and walking only four.
Weissert figures to be the leader in the clubhouse to take over Slaten's role in the bullpen.
A trio of injured options
The Red Sox have several pitchers looking to return from the injured list before the end of the regular season who could factor into the team's playoff push, including 2025 Cy Young Award runner-up Garrett Crochet, 2024 All-Star Tanner Houck, and Johan Oviedo.
Crochet
The 27-year-old ace has thrown four bullpen sessions since restarting a throwing progression on Aug. 3, with his most recent outing, a 30-pitch up-and-down session on the Fenway Park mound, coming on Tuesday afternoon. While Crochet, if healthy enough to appear in games, will almost certainly be on the postseason roster, he is expected to make multi-inning appearances rather than one-inning spurts like Slaten had been used, making him a valuable weapon but an imperfect replacement.
Houck
The now-30-year-old right-hander is attempting to return to the Boston staff in a "Swiss Army knife" role after undergoing Tommy John surgery in August 2025. Houck has already made three rehab appearances with both Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester, allowing two earned runs on one hit, walking four, and striking out seven in 4.2 innings. He is expected to return to Worcester on Saturday for a 40-50 pitch outing before potentially rejoining the Red Sox.
Though what exactly Houck can contribute after being out of major league action since May 2025 remains to be seen.
Oviedo
A bit of a forgotten man in the 2026 Red Sox season is the 28-year-old right-hander, who made only one appearance before landing on the injured list on April 3 with right elbow inflammation. Oviedo will make his first rehab appearance Thursday night with Worcester before deciding on next steps; at this point, the risk likely outweighs the reward of making the postseason roster.
Tracy, Breslow, and the rest of Boston's decision makers will have 10 games to make their final decisions on how exactly the postseason roster will look, and who will replace Slaten's high-leverage innings.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to avoid the sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers in Thursday's series finale from Globe Life Field. Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.76 ERA) gets the start for Boston opposite Tyler Alexander (5-2, 3.38 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are still sitting comfortably in the second Wild Card spot, but there are several issues they must resolve before they start thinking about playoff baseball.
Boston is a mediocre 11-11 over its last 22 games. While that's been good enough to sustain its playoff position, its play hasn't exactly inspired optimism for a deep postseason run.
Most of the Red Sox' problems can be linked to their underperforming lineup. Key hitters like Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Wilyer Abreu have been concerningly inconsistent.
A deeper dive into the numbers suggests the struggling Sox will have their work cut out for them in their presumed Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium. Here are the club's five biggest areas of concern with 10 games remaining:
Roman Anthony is ice-cold
The Red Sox need Roman Anthony to be one of their best offensive players to have any chance of a deep postseason run. If the former No. 1 prospect continues to play the way he has for most of September, that will be problematic.
Anthony is hitting just .149 (7-for-47) with one home run and a .428 OPS over his last 11 games. He has struck out 18 times in 51 plate appearances.
The 22-year-old's struggles beg the question: should he still be the leadoff hitter in the postseason? Interim manager Chad Tracy will have no choice but to reevaluate Anthony's spot in the lineup if his woes continue. The problem with that is there aren't any exciting alternatives. The leadoff spot has been a glaring issue all season long, regardless of who has been thrust into the role.
Struggling against high velocity
The Red Sox offense has been inconsistent no matter who's on the mound, but it has mostly struggled against pitchers with high velo. Here's how some of Boston's regulars have fared this season against pitches greater than or equal to 97 mph:
- Wilyer Abreu: .170 BA, .623 OPS (237 pitches)
- Jarren Duran: .065 BA, .300 OPS (203 pitches)
- Willson Contreras: .170 BA, .512 OPS (166 pitches)
- Ceddanne Rafaela: .205 BA, .449 OPS (157 pitches)
- Roman Anthony: .091 BA, .440 OPS (58 pitches)
- Adley Rutschman: .077 BA, .451 OPS (57 pitches)
The Red Sox' top performer against high velocity (97 mph and above) has been Caleb Durbin (.364 BA, .912 OPS, 161 pitches).
Being so vulnerable against high velocity will especially be a problem for Boston in its expected Wild Card Series matchup against the New York Yankees. Cy Young frontrunner and likely Game 1 starter Cam Schlittler averages 98 mph with his four-seam fastball, which he uses 44.5 percent of the time. Gerrit Cole averages 96.9 mph with his four-seam, using it 49.3 percent of the time.
Leaving runners stranded
Boston has been below average all season at capitalizing on runners in scoring position. It currently ranks 17th in batting average (.250) and 21st in OPS (.731) with RISP. They're hitting just .212 in such situations through 14 games so far in September.
The Yankees' elite pitching staff probably won't provide the Red Sox with many scoring opportunities in their short series, so it's imperative that they come through when given the chance. Lately, Boston hasn't had anyone in its lineup to feel confident about when they step to the plate with runners on.
Role players regressing
As great as guys like Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and Wilyer Abreu were throughout the Red Sox' incredible midseason turnaround, it was the role players who powered their surge. Mickey Gasper, Jahmai Jones, Nick Sogard, Anthony Seigler, and Andruw Monasterio were instrumental in resurrecting Boston's season.
Gasper has cooled off, though no one expected him to sustain his Barry Bonds-like run. Jahmai Jones is 4 for his last 22 (.182) with nine strikeouts, suddenly making him a playoff roster cut candidate. Sogard is still hitting, but his .758 OPS so far in September suggests regression to the mean. Seigler is hurt. Monasterio posted a .578 OPS in August and is 0-for-11 so far in September, putting him on the playoff roster bubble.
That group deserves immense credit for getting the Red Sox here, but it cannot be counted on to propel the club through the postseason.
Erik Miller experiencing command issues
Boston's bullpen is arguably its biggest strength heading into the postseason. The back end with Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Aroldis Chapman is elite.
We would've included trade deadline addition Erik Miller in that group last month, when he allowed only one earned run with 20 strikeouts and just three walks across his first 11 appearances with the Red Sox. His performance so far this month, however, has been alarming.
Miller, acquired from the San Francisco Giants in the Marcelo Mayer trade, has allowed four earned runs with six walks and six strikeouts through five appearances (4.1 IP) in September. His command struggles were a question mark upon his joining the club, and it appears that issue has reemerged with less than two weeks until the playoffs.
After Wednesday's poor outing against the Texas Rangers (2 H, 3 ER, 1 BB), Miller attributed his recent struggles to his mechanics. The Red Sox will hope that whatever the problem is, it's a quick fix, because Miller will be counted on to be their most reliable left-handed reliever not named Aroldis Chapman.

With 10 games left to play in the 2026 MLB regular season, the Milwaukee Brewers are 95-57 and, once again, have the best record in baseball. They have already clinched their fourth-consecutive National League Central Division crown and are still playing for the top seed in the playoffs.
Indeed, a great deal went right for Milwaukee this year, not the least of which being the emergence of Jacob Misiorowski has arguably the best pitcher in the game. After stumbling down the stretch and getting moved to the bullpen in 2025, Misiorowski now is poised to be the Brewers' Game One starter in each postsesaon series that they play.
MLB analyst admits he was wrong about Milwaukee Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski
Milwaukee selected the lanky Misiorowski in the second round of the 2022 MLB Draft. Four years later, he is their ace and a two-time NL All-Star.
There were not many who thought that the 2026 NL Cy Young favorite would be a successful Major League pitcher, though. One of them was Keith Law of The Athletic, who felt that Misiorowski was going to have control issues his whole professional career and/or blow out his arm.
On Thursday morning, he published an article about current Major League players that he was wrong about as prospects. The first one he discusses was Misiorowski.
He wrote, in part:
"I know I wasn't alone in my belief that Misiorowski wouldn't hold up as a starter, either because he wouldn't throw enough strikes or because he would break down. No one has ever thrown this hard, this much, without getting hurt.
"The delivery was still quite rough, and even with the benefit of some of the best stuff in the minors, he still walked almost 15 percent of batters during his time in Double A in 2023 and 2024. He was so inefficient that he'd hit his pitch limits before getting through five innings in the majority of his outings.
"I thought any team would try to smooth out Miz's delivery, but that either it would cost him velocity — that the power was the result of the violence, not held back by it, because who thinks a guy throwing 100 could actually be throwing harder if he had better mechanics? — or that it wouldn't improve his control enough to keep him a starter. Obviously, that didn't end up being the case. His delivery and command improved and he maintained his elite velocity."
Law credits both Misiorowski's desire to improve and the Brewers' organizational coaches for identifying ways to help him improve his command and stay healthy while throwing harder than any starting pitcher in the pitch-tracking era.
The work that Milwaukee has done sure has paid off. With 1-2 starts left in the season, the Brewers ace is 15-5 with a Major League-best 1.89 ERA, 243 strikeouts, and .081 WHIP.
If he is able to maintain the dominance he was shown all year long, and keep opposing hitters from making consistent contact in his final start(s), Misiorowski will set yet another Major League record. Currently, opposing batters are hitting .160 off of him, which is the lowest mark for a starter in baseball history.
Misiorowski proved his doubters wrong. Now, Milwaukee as a team hopes they can do the same by making it to the World Series for the first time since 1982, and winning it for the first time ever.
